title: Looking back: the Gurus' teachings
hook: Nanak's dialogues, the Gurus' voices, the Ninth's calm
tomorrow: Looking back: the Tenth Guru's pen

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the ragas: one Word sung in every mood. Your line was many moods. When your mood shifted, what music did it need? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

In a hymn by Guru Nanak, there's his name: Nanak. In a hymn by Guru Arjan, a later Guru, the same name appears: Nanak. Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Tegh Bahadur: the Gurus whose hymns fill the Granth sign them as Nanak. To a newcomer, it can look like a mistake in the credits. To Sikhs, it's the point. Yesterday the year's look back was about the music. Today it's about the voices, how different they sound, and why they're signed with one name.
screen: `SIGNED: NANAK.` → `A DIFFERENT GURU, THE SAME NAME.` → `NOT A MISTAKE. THE POINT.`

segments.voice: First, Nanak in dialogue. Guru Nanak doesn't only sing; he argues, gently. In the Sidh Gosht, yogis who have left the world question him: why stay among householders? His answers keep returning to the Word, and to living truthfully in the world rather than fleeing it. Teaching, for him, could be a conversation. Second, how you tell the voices apart. Each hymn carries a heading, Mahala one, Mahala two and so on, marking which Guru composed it, while the signature stays Nanak. Listen across them: Guru Angad's spare sloks, Guru Amar Das's Anand, Guru Arjan's long Sukhmani. Different temperaments. One signature. Third, the Ninth Guru's calm. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns have a stillness all their own. In Raag Sorath he describes, in paraphrase, the person who isn't shaken by pain, isn't carried off by pleasure, holds praise and blame alike, and sees gold as dust. It reads like the voice of someone who has already let go. Fourth, why one name. In the ballad of Balwand and Satta, they sing, in paraphrase, that the light was the same and the way was the same; only the body changed. Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light passing from lamp to lamp. And around them, the bhagats, Kabir, Farid, Namdev and others, keep their own names, welcomed in. Many voices. It's a picture of a good conversation: different people, saying the truth in their own way, without needing to drown each other out.
screen: `NANAK IN DIALOGUE: THE SIDH GOSHT.` · `MAHALA: WHICH GURU IS SPEAKING.` · `THE NINTH GURU'S CALM.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP TO LAMP.` · then, large: `MANY VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one teaching. Settle, and breathe. Here are three, from three voices, in paraphrase. Guru Nanak: stay in the world, and live truthfully in it. Guru Arjan: all are sharers, and God is outside of no one. Guru Tegh Bahadur: hold praise and blame alike. Let one of them choose you. Then say it slowly to yourself, once on the in-breath, once on the out-breath, and let it settle. If you have a Granth or a translation nearby, you can find the hymn later and read it whole. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. At the year's close, the Gurus' teachings: different voices, each hymn marked by its Mahala, all signed Nanak, one light passed on. Today's word.
Your line: many voices. Today, in one conversation, let someone finish saying the truth their own way before you say yours. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing the hymns of the Gurus and the bhagats together in the Guru Granth Sahib; each hymn's heading names its raga and its Mahala, which tells readers which Guru composed it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Granth is one author's book.

notes: The Gurus whose hymns are in the Granth sign as 'Nanak', with Mahala headings marking the Guru; please confirm wording ('Mahala one, Mahala two and so on').

Sidh Gosht summary (yogis question why he lives among householders; answers return to the Word and truthful living in the world) is a broad paraphrase; please confirm. Day 1402 used the Sidh Gosht's lotus-and-duck image, which is avoided here.
Ang 633: please confirm 'jo nar dukh mai dukh nahi manai' and the paraphrase (unshaken by pain and pleasure, praise and blame alike, gold as dust).
Ang 966: please confirm 'joti oha jugati sai sahi kaia pheri paltiai' and the paraphrase.
'Through the year you've heard Guru Angad's sloks, Guru Amar Das's Anand, Guru Arjan's Sukhmani' assumes these were taught this year; please check against the year-4 outline.
'Guru Arjan, a different man, born much later': no date given; please confirm phrasing.
